articles.title: WRITE FOR HUMANS. GET FOUND BY AI.
articles.summary:
For (at least) the last two years, marketers have been told to optimize for AI: lead with answers, add FAQs, eliminate the adjectives.

But when machine readability comes at the expense of voice, insight, and originality, the result may be easy to parse, and easy to ignore.

Write for Humans, Not AI [5]is Markup AI's framework for B2B marketing teams using AI to scale content production without losing what makes their brand worth reading. Learn where AI belongs in the content process, where human judgment matters most, and how to check whether a piece is genuinely ready to publish.

ATTENTION IS RENTED. MEMORY IS THE NEW MEDIA
articles.summary: Reach and impressions show who saw a campaign, not what they remember. 47% of industry leaders say experiential marketing's value comes from long-term brand memory. Emotional intensity and physical presence can help brands cut through crowded digital feeds. The strongest activations create stories people keep talking about rather than generating a short-lived spike in attention. Brands are increasingly using physical experiences to turn campaigns into lasting cultural moments.

articles.title: THE WELLBEING EDIT: HOW TEENS ARE USING PINTEREST DIFFERENTLY, BY DESIGN
articles.summary: Teens use Pinterest more intentionally than traditional social platforms. Re-Pins per user are up 64%, searches are up 44%, and board organization is up 68%. More than 77% proactively search to explore interests, while teens use feed and settings controls nearly 2X more than other age groups. Pinterest is positioning itself around inspiration and identity exploration rather than social performance, with art searches 1.26X higher among teens.

articles.title: HOW I BUILT AN SEO/AEO BLOG ENGINE
articles.summary: A growth engineering intern at Browserbase built an AI engine to automate its SEO and AEO workflow. 53% of search traffic came from just five posts, while only 17 of 77 posts had been cited by AI engines. BlogEO audits existing content, finds search opportunities, generates drafts, and tracks AI citations. Human approval remains in the loop. After 6 weeks, search impressions grew 5.8X, page-one queries grew 9.8X, and average blog position improved from 10.9 to 6.6.

articles.title: HOW TO GIVE AWAY FREE PRODUCT AND MAKE MONEY DOING IT
articles.summary: Lovable treats free AI product usage as acquisition spend rather than a margin drain, measured against a 3-month payback threshold weighing conversion, retention, and expansion. That framing matters more now that AI has pushed gross margins from the SaaS era's 80-90% toward 40% or less, leading many companies to gate AI functionality behind paywalls instead of letting users experience it first. Free-to-paid conversion for Lovable runs 5-10%, and partner-driven giveaways with a strong audience match can convert at 40-60%. The realistic alternative to giving the product away is spending far more to acquire the same customers through paid channels, not keeping the money.

articles.title: GOOGLE IS COMING FOR THE FREE TOOLS SMALL WEBSITES DEPEND ON
articles.summary: Google can now generate a calculator, converter, or other interactive tool directly inside AI Overviews and AI Mode, expanded globally in English this August. Small utility sites built around one simple public formula, one input and one output, are the easiest target for a model to assemble on the spot.

articles.title: THE 11X ROAS ACCOUNT THAT LOST MONEY ON EVERY ORDER
articles.summary: An account reporting an 11x return on ad spend was losing money on every order once returns, VAT, cost of goods, and fulfillment came out of what the platform called conversion value. Much of that 11x came from brand campaigns near 18x, largely shoppers who had already decided to buy, blended with a real nonbrand return closer to 3x. Correcting for margin alone created a second problem, since bidding purely for efficiency starved an apparel SKU of volume, leaving more stock to mark down below cost at season's end. The fix was rebuilding conversion values around actual contribution and giving each SKU one deliberate job, for profit, for volume, or for cash back before the season closed.

articles.title: THE AFTERMARKET PREMIUM
articles.summary: The aftermarket can become a major source of value around durable products and platforms, so platform owners must decide whether to coexist, fight, license, or buy the businesses that emerge around them. AMG shows how licensing and acquisition can bring a successful modifier inside the brand, while Rolex's service restrictions show that fighting can leave substantial margin and customer demand to independent players. In software, platform owners control whether an aftermarket can legally form through decisions about open source, licensing, and developer tools, which helped create businesses like Counter Strike, Red Hat, and Cursor.

articles.title: SEEING LIKE A STATE
articles.summary: Dashboards make marketing easier to measure, but they can also hide the work that actually drives growth. Teams may optimize for traffic or output while overlooking customer knowledge and relationship-building. These efforts are harder to quantify but can have a bigger long-term impact. Treat metrics as incomplete maps and question what each dashboard leaves out. Regularly compare the data with what customers and teams are seeing firsthand.
